---
title: "Part 2. — Computing for Research"
subtitle: "From scripts to reproducible research software"
---

## Purpose

This stage develops the computing foundation needed for the rest of the programme using Python. The goal is not merely to *use Python*, but to write research code that is readable, tested, reproducible and suitable for extension into machine-learning research.
It is a 10-week programme covering Python, NumPy, pandas, Polars, SQL, scikit-learn, PyTorch, Linux/shell, Git, testing, packaging and reproducible research software. I have used current online resources freely available, including Harvard CS50P, MIT's 2026 Missing Semester, Harvard CS50 SQL, and the current NumPy/pandas/Polars/PyTorch/scikit-learn documentation. CS50P can be completed using its browser-based development environment; MIT's 2026 Missing Semester includes recorded lectures on shell, Git, debugging, packaging and code quality. The current technical documentation also reflects recent versions of NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn and PyTorch.

**Suggested duration:** 10 weeks  
**Workload:** 10–12 hours per week

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this stage, you should be able to:

- write idiomatic Python using functions, modules, classes, type hints and exceptions;
- work efficiently with NumPy arrays and vectorised numerical computation;
- clean, reshape and analyse data with pandas and Polars;
- query relational data using SQL, including joins, CTEs and window functions;
- use the scikit-learn estimator and pipeline APIs correctly;
- use PyTorch tensors, datasets, automatic differentiation and basic modules;
- work comfortably in a shell and use Git/GitHub for version control;
- structure, test, document and package a small research project;
- reproduce a complete empirical workflow from raw data to final results.

## Core courses

### Harvard — CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python

[Course website](https://cs50.harvard.edu/python/)

Use this selectively rather than treating it as a compulsory ten-week course. Prioritise:

- functions and variables;
- exceptions;
- libraries;
- unit tests;
- file I/O;
- object-oriented programming.

The course can be completed using the browser-based `cs50.dev` environment, so a local Python installation is not essential.

### MIT — The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (2026)

[Course website and videos](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/)

Prioritise:

- shell and command-line environment;
- development environments and tools;
- debugging and profiling;
- Git;
- packaging and shipping code;
- code quality.

### Harvard — CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL

[Course website](https://cs50.harvard.edu/sql/)

For this stage, complete the material on:

- querying;
- relating tables;
- database design;
- views;
- indexes and optimisation.

## Week-by-week plan

| Week | Topic | Core work | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Shell, Git and Python workflow | Terminal navigation, files, processes, Git commits/branches, Python execution, environments | Create a clean research repository |
| **2** | Python as a programming language | Functions, scope, modules, iterators, exceptions, classes, type hints, file handling | Refactor one old research script into modules |
| **3** | NumPy and numerical computing | Arrays, shapes, indexing, broadcasting, vectorisation, random generators, linear algebra, copies/views | Reimplement common econometric matrix operations |
| **4** | pandas for empirical research | Import/export, selection, joins, groupby, reshaping, missing data, categorical data, dates, validation | Clean and construct an analysis-ready panel dataset |
| **5** | Polars and efficient data workflows | Expressions, lazy execution, query optimisation, joins, group operations, Parquet/Arrow | Reproduce Week 4 in Polars and benchmark it |
| **6** | SQL and relational data | SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, CTEs, subqueries, window functions, keys, normalisation, indexes | Build and query a small relational economic database |
| **7** | scikit-learn as a software framework | Estimators, transformers, preprocessing, `Pipeline`, `ColumnTransformer`, train/test discipline | Build a leakage-safe predictive pipeline |
| **8** | PyTorch foundations | Tensors, NumPy interoperability, `Dataset`, `DataLoader`, `nn.Module`, autograd, optimisation loop | Implement linear regression in PyTorch |
| **9** | Research software engineering | `pytest`, assertions, typing, logging, configuration, profiling, package layout, `pyproject.toml` | Convert the project into a tested Python package |
| **10** | Reproducibility capstone | End-to-end data pipeline, CLI/script entry point, documentation, environment specification, Git release | Publish the Stage 1 capstone repository |

## Essential technical references

### Python

Python Software Foundation. *The Python Tutorial*.  
[Official documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/)

For deeper Python practice:

Ramalho, L. (2022). *Fluent Python* (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

### NumPy

NumPy Developers. *NumPy User Guide*.  
[Official user guide](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/)

Focus on:

- array creation;
- indexing;
- broadcasting;
- data types;
- copies and views;
- universal functions;
- linear algebra.

### pandas

pandas Development Team. *pandas User Guide*.  
[Official user guide](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/)

Focus on:

- indexing;
- merge/join;
- reshaping;
- missing data;
- `groupby`;
- window operations;
- time series;
- performance.

A useful book is:

McKinney, W. (2022). *Python for Data Analysis: Data Wrangling with pandas, NumPy, and Jupyter* (3rd ed.). O'Reilly Media.

### Polars

Polars Contributors. *Polars User Guide*.  
[Official documentation](https://docs.pola.rs/)

Start with the [pandas-to-Polars migration guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/migration/pandas/). Do not simply translate pandas syntax line by line: learn the Polars expression model and lazy API.

### SQL

PostgreSQL Global Development Group. *PostgreSQL Documentation: Tutorial*.  
[Official tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial.html)

You should be comfortable with:

```sql
SELECT
FROM
WHERE
JOIN
GROUP BY
HAVING
WITH
CASE
OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
```

### scikit-learn

scikit-learn Developers. *scikit-learn User Guide*.  
[Official user guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

For Stage 1, concentrate on software structure rather than ML theory:

```python
Pipeline
ColumnTransformer
fit
transform
predict
```

Model selection and statistical learning are treated properly in Stage 2.

### PyTorch

PyTorch Contributors. *Learn the Basics — PyTorch Tutorials*.  
[Official tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/)

Complete:

- tensors;
- datasets and dataloaders;
- building a model;
- automatic differentiation;
- optimisation;
- saving/loading models.

Deep-learning theory begins in Stage 4.

### Git

Chacon, S., & Straub, B. (2014). *Pro Git* (2nd ed.). Apress.  
[Free online edition](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2)

## Coding standard

From this stage onwards, avoid repositories consisting mainly of one large notebook.

Prefer:

```text
project/
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/
│   └── project_name/
├── tests/
├── notebooks/
├── scripts/
├── data/
└── results/
```

Use notebooks primarily for exploration and exposition. Put reusable functions and substantive computational logic in `src/`.

## Stage 1 capstone

Rebuild one empirical economics project as a reproducible research-software project.

A suitable workflow is:

```text
raw data
   ↓
SQL / structured storage
   ↓
Python extraction and validation
   ↓
pandas or Polars transformation
   ↓
NumPy / statistical computation
   ↓
scikit-learn or PyTorch demonstration
   ↓
tables and figures
   ↓
automated tests
   ↓
documented GitHub repository
```

### Minimum requirements

The repository must include:

- a clear `README.md`;
- a reproducible environment;
- raw-to-analysis data scripts;
- reusable code under `src/`;
- at least five meaningful automated tests;
- no undocumented manual data-cleaning steps;
- at least one SQL query involving multiple tables;
- at least one vectorised NumPy operation;
- one pandas/Polars data pipeline;
- one minimal scikit-learn or PyTorch example;
- a tagged Git release.

## Completion criterion

Do not move to Stage 2 merely because all videos have been watched.

Stage 1 is complete when you can take an unfamiliar empirical dataset and independently build a repository that another researcher can clone, understand and reproduce without asking you how your code works.
